definition: Squander means to waste something valuable recklessly — to spend money, time, or a chance on nothing worth having.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word squander. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know squander should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The team squandered a three-goal lead in the final period, giving the puck away at center ice again and again.
Waste is weaker than squander: any slack afternoon can waste an hour, but to squander is to burn through something precious with both hands, and the loss stings.
Hemorrhage goes further than squander — a squandered budget was thrown away choice by choice, while a hemorrhaging one is bleeding out faster than anyone can even track.

To fritter something away is to waste it in small nibbles — a dollar here, ten minutes there — until it is quietly gone. Squander moves in bigger, more reckless strokes: the fortune, the lead, the once-in-a-lifetime chance, thrown away in full view.

To dissipate money or energy is to scatter it until nothing is left, often in idle pleasure. Dissipate watches the resource thin out and vanish; squander points at the person — it is an accusation of reckless, blameworthy waste.

The trail behind squander is short and cold: it appears in Elizabethan English meaning 'to scatter,' with no known parent word before it and no descendants after. Etymologists' best guess is a lost dialect word, possibly a cousin of 'wander' in shape only. Its family tree is a single tree.

Historians still wince at how the expedition squandered its head start: three weeks of perfect weather spent renaming landmarks and staging photographs, while the pass ahead quietly filled with snow.

Squander is harsher than 'waste' because it adds blame and scale: something genuinely valuable — three weeks of perfect weather — was thrown away recklessly by the very people who held it, and it will not come back.
Squander comes with the blame built in: it accuses someone of recklessly throwing away something precious — a fortune, a lead, a one-time chance.
Deplete just tracks a supply going down, with no judgment attached, and waste covers even trivial losses.
Reach for squander when the loss was valuable, avoidable, and someone's fault.

The Whitfield bequest was the largest gift the county museum had ever received — enough, the papers said, to secure its collections for a generation.
The new director had other ideas.
Within eighteen months the money had gone to a marble lobby, a rebranded logo, and a gala that flew in a celebrity chef.
Meanwhile the roof over the textile hall kept leaking, and two conservators left for lack of funds.
The board's review did not mince words: the director had squandered the bequest — a once-in-a-generation resource spent recklessly on show, with nothing lasting to point to.
The lobby gleams; the collections it was meant to protect sit under plastic sheeting.
